nameStory: Timothy grass gets its name from Timothy Hanson, an American farmer who promoted this European grass in the early 1700s. He recognized its value as hay and helped spread it throughout colonial America, where it became so associated with his name that "timothy" stuck. Some also call it "cat's tail" because its dense, cylindrical flower spike looks remarkably like a fuzzy cat's tail.
description: Timothy grass is a sturdy perennial grass that forms dense clumps and can grow 2-4 feet tall. Originally from Europe, it's now one of New England's most common grasses, especially in fields and meadows. Its most distinctive feature is a tight, cylindrical flower spike that looks like a fuzzy green or purplish cattail on top of a straight stem. The leaves are flat and ribbon-like, typical of many grasses, but timothy's compact flower head makes it easy to spot.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cylindrical spike 2-6 inches long that feels soft and fuzzy to the touch, resembling a cat's tail. The spike is packed with tiny flowers and often has a greenish to purplish color.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Flat, narrow blades that are smooth on top but slightly rough on the underside when you run your finger along them. They're typically 4-8 inches long and about a quarter-inch wide.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms clumps or bunches rather than spreading by runners. Stems stand upright and are smooth and round, feeling firm but not woody when squeezed.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds that shake out of the fuzzy flower spike when mature, making a subtle rattling sound if you tap the dried seed head in late summer.

habitat: Timothy thrives in open fields, meadows, pastures, and along roadsides throughout New England. It prefers rich, moist soils but tolerates a wide range of conditions from sea level to mountain valleys. You'll often find it mixed with clover, dandelions, and other common field plants in both wild and cultivated grasslands.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge early, forming distinctive clumps. Young leaves are tender and bright green.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the characteristic fuzzy flower spikes appear, usually from June through August. The spikes start green and may turn purplish as they mature.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes dry out and turn brown, but often persist on stems. Seeds scatter and leaves begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems and dried flower heads may remain standing through snow, appearing as brown stubble in dormant fields.

funFact: Timothy grass was so valuable for feeding horses that it helped fuel westward expansion in America – pioneer families would scatter timothy seed as they traveled, creating instant hay fields for their livestock at stopping points along the way.
confusionNotes: Timothy is most often confused with foxtail grasses, but timothy's flower spike feels soft and fuzzy while foxtails have bristly, rough spikes that can irritate your skin. Memory trick: Timothy is "timid and soft" while foxtails are "fierce and prickly."
contextualKnowledge: Despite being non-native, timothy grass is so well-established in New England that it's considered naturalized rather than invasive. It's still widely planted as hay and is one of the most economically important grasses in the region for livestock feed.
compareHints: Timothy differs from its mountain-dwelling relative Alpine Timothy by being much taller and having longer flower spikes. Alpine Timothy stays under 2 feet tall and has shorter, more egg-shaped flower heads, plus it only grows at high elevations. Timothy's robust size and lowland habitat make it the species you're most likely to encounter in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Alpine Timothy differs from its common relative Timothy grass by being much shorter, more compact, and restricted to harsh mountain environments.
